probe.format_note: Single 9:16 film, 720x1280, 30 fps, 3729 frames (124.3 s video), container 124.39 s, about 636 kb/s. Audio: HE-AAC stereo 44.1 kHz, continuous for the whole film (no silence of 0.4 s or more below -45 dB), mean -16.8 dB, peak -0.7 dB. The word-by-word captions imply narration; the audio was measured only, not listened to or analysed for beats; third-party audio never reused.

mode.why: third-party film of unknown origin: borrow the motion language, data-on-screen system and look only, never its shots one by one, its subject, its copy or its figures (owner note); the reference is a narrated data explainer (common belief → worked example → the mistake named → experiment → formula and chart → second example → consequence → payoff → CTA), so EXPLAINER fits; a hook/problem/solution package may still run as REEL in this style

ignored.why: the subject (driving speed, time saved, braking distance, the named cognitive bias) and every Persian caption, headline, pill, label and chart note are third-party copy and claims; never reused as voice-over, on-screen text or story

all figures (speeds, route length, times, seconds saved, deltas, braking metres, percentages) are third-party claims; only the way numbers count, compare and appear is borrowed, our numbers come from the approved package

the scenery and props (road, pine forest and hills, cars, reflector posts, village houses, racing lanes and finish gate, roadworks barrier and cones, crash) are the reference's story; our scenes take their subjects from the voice-over and are only drawn in this rendering style
the logo card, its extruded third-party logo and the Follow button belong to the third-party channel; our end uses the brand's own CTA and logo outro
the red-orange colour is the reference's accent; it is mapped onto the brand's colour roles, only its role (one hot accent over near-black) is kept
the audio track is third-party; L2/L6 use our own voice and sound

method: ffprobe; ffmpeg contact sheets fps=2, 480 px, tile 4x3 (21 sheets, all viewed); scene detect gt(scene,0.3) and gt(scene,0.12) (cuts at 5.5, 15.6, 27.1, 33.1, 51.3, 72.07, 86.6, 95.13, 104.4, 110.2, 115.2, 118.93; 109.7 is the impact flash inside a shot, 33.13 is the same cut as 33.1, 62.17 at score 0.13 is not a cut, 104.4 was found only at the lower threshold, max score 0.97 at 5.5); dense sheets fps=10 over 5.2-6.4 s, 15.2-16.4 s and 109.2-111.0 s, fps=5 over 1.4-3.8 s (all viewed). Spans from scene detect where a cut exists, in-shot beat times from the 2 fps sheets (about ±0.25 s), so durations outside the dense windows are estimates. silencedetect + volumedetect on the audio. Colours read by eye, not sampled. The video was never watched in motion: easing is inferred from frame spacing.

visual_language: Narrated data explainer in one real-3D low-poly world, cut like a continuous lesson: 13 shots in 124.4 s, average about 9.6 s (range 3.7-20.8 s), far longer than the usual reel because each shot holds many beats instead of cuts. New information lands about every 0.5-2 s through words, counters, pops and camera moves, all timed to the caption, not to a music beat. Two sets alternate: a story set (road or terrain with actors) for examples, and a neutral stage (horizon silhouette, red glow, floating low-poly rocks, faceted ground) for ideas and data, so the film breathes between concrete and abstract. Typography is one system: (1) a flat bold white caption with soft shadow and no pill at about 79% height, centred, 3-7 words, karaoke: spoken words white, the current word accent, coming words grey, with an occasional second line; (2) extruded 3D words and numerals with a pale side and motion smear that live in world space and turn with the camera, pinned to the object they describe; (3) a dark translucent rounded scoreboard fixed at the top of the frame, two or four columns, tiny label over big digits; (4) solid accent pills with a soft glow for the result, plus a dark outlined pill for the surprise; (5) dark 3D slab cards and a solid accent rectangle stamp; (6) a thin glowing accent progress line on the very top edge growing right-to-left. Moves: long smooth flying camera moves with heavy ease-in-out, slow drifts while data runs, pops with slight overshoot (about 0.2-0.3 s), counters and draws in step with the words. Palette: near-black, deep maroon and warm brown under a saturated red-orange horizon glow; one hot accent for what matters now, beige as the neutral comparison colour, white for text. Signature moments: the opening orbit from front to behind the actors; the whip tilt into a top-down map through a grey veil; the path painted hot section by section; the experiment with a counting scoreboard; the ball walking a curve; the second curve overturning the first; the impact with a red flash and a slow tumble; the small number leading to a big one.
look: Real 3D (not flat), low-poly and flat-shaded with hard facet edges and no bevels, matte materials, faceted terrain where each triangle catches a different value, a few emissive lines (the accent curve, the painted path). Light: one low warm sun behind the scene giving a saturated red-orange horizon band and very long hard shadows on the ground, plus actors' own light cones (soft warm white pools with visible translucent beam shapes). Strong vignette: the top of the sky and the bottom of the ground fall almost to black. Shadows are hard and long on the story set, soft blobs under floating objects on the stage. Depth: real perspective and aerial layering, mild blur on the far distance, motion blur and smear during fast camera moves and on extruded type, foreground props passing close to the lens. Background: vertical gradient sky (black to maroon to hot red-orange at the horizon) over dark layered silhouettes, with floating low-poly rocks on the stage.
code_translation: Built as real 3D in code with three.js (D55), never flattened: low-poly models from BoxGeometry, ConeGeometry, DodecahedronGeometry and displaced PlaneGeometry terrain, all with flatShading matte MeshStandardMaterial; InstancedMesh for forests or crowds of small props; one low DirectionalLight for long hard shadows (high resolution shadow map, low sun angle) plus a warm SpotLight on each actor and a translucent additive cone for the visible beam; sky as a large gradient plane or shader in brand colour roles, fog for layering, a vignette and mild bloom in post (UnrealBloomPass on emissive only). Camera: a CatmullRomCurve3 path per shot with look-at targets, eased with a strong in-out curve; frame-blend motion blur on fast moves; the whip as a fast tilt with a hard cut and a grey veil (flat pale grey overlay at about 50% opacity, cleared in about 0.2-0.3 s). Extruded 3D words and numerals: Persian text shaped first (HarfBuzz or the canvas) into outlines, then ExtrudeGeometry with a pale side material, so joins stay correct; numerals switch to a new mesh per value or use a texture on the front face, with Persian digits per data-viz.md; a directional smear via a short trail or frame blend. Scoreboard, pills, cards labels and captions as HTML/canvas overlay in the brand Persian font: caption with word-by-word highlight synced to audio.json word times, counters driven from the same timeline, labels projected from 3D anchors (Vector3.project) each frame. Painted path: a ribbon along the curve with an emissive material and a rough leading edge through a shader mask, advanced by section. Chart: instanced boxes with scale.y on a stagger, a TubeGeometry with drawRange or a growing tube for the curve, a sphere moved by curve.getPointAt. Bars and slab cards as thin boxes with shadows in the scene. Impact: an accent overlay flash and rigid pieces thrown with a simple velocity and slow time. Top progress line as an overlay driven by film time, growing from right to left per rtl-grammar.md.
continuity: One world, one light: every shot, story or abstract, sits in the same dusk light, horizon glow and faceted ground, so hard cuts still feel like one place.
Two alternating sets: concrete examples in a story set, ideas and data on a neutral stage, and the switch itself marks a change of thinking.
The grey veil: most cuts land on a flat pale grey wash that clears in about 0.2-0.3 s, one repeated device that reads as a page turn and hides set changes.
Whip into a new viewpoint: the camera accelerates into empty sky, cuts, and settles on the new view, so the move carries across the cut.
Tags live on their subject: a value stays attached to the object in world space through orbits and pushes, so the viewer never loses which number belongs to what.
Fixed data overlay: a scoreboard stays in the same screen place while the camera moves underneath, and it keeps its values until the next idea, so results accumulate.
Everything grows from the world: bars, columns and cards rise out of the ground of the current shot rather than appearing as a separate graphic layer.
One orbit tells the comparison: a single continuous camera move shows the same two subjects from front, side and behind instead of cutting between them.
Word-locked changes: a colour, a pop, a counter stop or a chart step lands on the word the caption is highlighting, so the caption drives the picture.
Replay with one change: the same scenario runs again from the same set with one variable altered, and the different ending is the argument.
Layered building: a small live model feeds a data bar that feeds a gauge, each new layer added above the last in the same frame.
Symbol callback: an object introduced early returns near the end in a new state that carries the conclusion.
A thread that keeps time: the progress line on the top edge runs across every cut.
A hero parked at the end: the main actor returns small and stays in the corner of the end card, closing the story without another shot.
risks: Third-party film of unknown origin: ADAPT only. Never copy its subject, any caption, headline, pill, label or chart note, its figures, its logo or handle, its audio, or its shot order one by one.

The film is 124 s, far longer than a usual reel: its average 9.6 s shot works because each shot holds many beats. On a short film keep the beat density and scale the moves down rather than keeping these long holds, or a shot with too few beats will look static.

Extruded Persian type needs correct shaping before extrusion and must stay readable when it turns with the camera; the reference lets it smear and tilt heavily, which breaks the readability rule at small sizes. Keep it large, limit the turn and hold it still for the required reading time.

Thin small text is frequent here (scoreboard labels, axis labels, small notes, far-off tags are tiny at 720x1280). Our film must meet the minimum sizes in safe-zones.md; enlarge them instead of copying the sizes.

The caption sits at about 79% height, and some layers (the dark chip at 73%, actors, cones, road lines) pass behind or very close to it; it has no pill, only a shadow, so contrast can drop over bright props. Check the safe zone and add a stronger shadow or scrim where needed.

The red-orange and maroon world is the reference's palette. Colours are mapped onto brand colour roles and may change the mood; keep the structure of one hot accent, a glowing horizon and near-black masses.

The grey veil is a flat wash and looks like a fade fault if overused or mistimed on a very short film; keep it at about 0.2-0.3 s and use plain cuts for dark-to-dark moments, as the reference does at 104.4 s and 118.93 s.
Real 3D with long shadows, instanced forests and frame-blend motion blur costs render time; budget samples and shadow map size, and reduce instance counts for props that are small on screen.

Timing outside the dense windows comes from 2 fps sheets (about ±0.25 s), and the easing is inferred from frame spacing without watching in motion; the audio was measured, not listened to. Sample a dense sheet before borrowing a specific move exactly.
A crash image is a strong device: use the impact pattern only when the voice-over calls for it, and never as decoration.
